system: You are a writer of plain, descriptive encyclopaedia-style prose.
message: Write about 2210 words on the natural and settlement history of a fictional river valley, the Aldern, from its geology to its villages, mills and bridges. This is part 1 of 4 of one continuous article; write only this part, continuing the account in order (part 1 begins at the valley's geology; part 4 ends with the present day). Write descriptive prose only: what things are, where, when, how they work physically, how they changed over time. Do NOT discuss evidence, research methods, how to reason, how to judge claims, reviewing, teamwork, collaboration, decision-making, advice, or controversies and debates. No lists, no headings beyond a title, no questions to the reader. Invent a fictional place where needed; do not cite studies or numbers from studies.

# The Aldern Valley

The Aldern is a river of moderate length that rises among the moorland heights of the Carrow Fells and runs for roughly forty miles south and east before it joins the broader Wenne below the market town of Selby Cross. Along its course it passes through three distinct kinds of country. In its upper reaches it is a fast upland stream cut into hard rock. Through its middle section it widens into a valley of meadows, woods and small fields. In its lower course it is a slow, looping river across a flat plain of silt and gravel. The settlements, mills, roads and bridges of the valley were shaped by these differences, and their history begins with the rocks.

The oldest rocks in the Aldern basin lie at its head. The summits of the Carrow Fells, including the long whaleback of High Carrow and the steeper crag-edged mass of Gallow Pike, are built of dark grey gritstone and mudstone laid down as sediment on the floor of an ancient sea. These beds were later buried, compressed and folded by slow movements of the earth's crust until they were tilted steeply and in places stood almost on edge. The gritstone is coarse and resistant, made of sand grains and small quartz pebbles cemented tightly together. The mudstones between its beds are softer and split readily into thin flakes. Where the two alternate on the fellsides, weathering has left the gritstone standing out as low scarps and ledges, while the mudstone has worn back into gentle hollows. From a distance the upper slopes therefore look stepped or ribbed, with lines of crag running across the hillsides like the courses of a ruined wall.

Downstream of the fells the river crosses onto a younger and quite different series of rocks. A broad band of pale limestone forms the country around the middle valley. It was laid down in a warm, shallow sea that once lapped against the older land of the Carrow highlands, and it is made largely of the crushed shells and skeletons of small marine creatures, with occasional beds packed with whole fossils of shellfish and the stems of sea lilies. The limestone is jointed into rough blocks by vertical cracks and horizontal bedding planes, and rainwater, which is faintly acidic, has widened many of these cracks as it seeps downward. On the open tops above the middle valley the rock surface is broken into clints and grikes, flat slabs divided by deep narrow fissures in which ferns and small woodland plants find shelter from wind and grazing animals. Beneath the surface the water has dissolved passages and caves, and several streams that rise on the fells sink into the limestone at swallow holes and run underground for a mile or more before reappearing as springs on the valley sides.

Above the limestone, and forming the lower slopes of the middle valley and the ridges that enclose it, lies a sequence of sandstones, shales and thin coal seams. These rocks were formed in swamps and river deltas that spread across the region after the limestone sea withdrew. The sandstones are buff or reddish brown, softer than the gritstone of the fells but strong enough for building, and they break into regular blocks that can be dressed into square stones. The shales are grey and crumbly, and where they are exposed in stream banks they slump easily. The coal seams are mostly thin and of poor quality in the Aldern basin, but here and there they outcrop on the hillsides as black streaks in the soil.

The lower valley rests on the youngest solid rocks of the basin, a series of soft red mudstones and sandstones laid down in a hot, dry age when much of the land was desert. These red beds weather quickly into fine soil and seldom form crags. Over most of the lower valley they are hidden beneath later deposits, and they appear only in the sides of deep lanes and in the cliffs that the river has cut into its outer bends, where they show as bright brick-red faces streaked with paler bands of sand.

The present form of the valley owes much to the ice ages. During the colder periods glaciers spread down from the Carrow Fells and filled the upper part of the basin. The ice moved slowly downhill under its own weight, dragging rock fragments along its base, and it scraped and deepened the existing stream valley into a broad trough with steep sides and a flatter floor. At the head of the Aldern, beneath the eastern face of Gallow Pike, a small glacier carved a deep armchair-shaped hollow known as Carrow Comb. When the ice melted, a small dark tarn was left in the bottom of the hollow, held in by a low ridge of boulders and gravel that the glacier had pushed up at its snout. The tarn, called Comb Water, is the highest standing water in the valley, and the river's first clear channel runs out of it through a gap in the boulder ridge.

Lower down, the glaciers left their burden of ground-up rock spread across the valley floor and lower slopes as a thick, stiff clay studded with stones of every size. This boulder clay covers much of the middle valley and gives its fields their heavy, slow-draining soils. In places the ice shaped the clay into smooth oval mounds, all aligned in the direction of the ice movement, so that the land between the villages of Hartshaw and Ewen Bridge has a rolling, egg-box appearance. Large boulders of gritstone carried down from the fells lie scattered across the limestone country, some of them perched on small pedestals of limestone where the surrounding rock has dissolved away around them since the ice retreated.

As the climate warmed and the ice wasted away, great quantities of meltwater poured down the valley. These floods carried sand and gravel far beyond the ice margin and laid them down across the lower valley in broad, flat spreads. Later, as the volume of water fell and the river settled into a narrower course, it cut down into these deposits and left parts of them standing as terraces along the valley sides. Two main terraces can be traced through much of the lower valley. The higher of them lies some way above the modern flood level and forms a dry, level bench of well-drained gravel; the lower one sits closer to the river and is occasionally reached by the highest floods. Below them both lies the modern floodplain, a ribbon of fine silt and clay laid down by the river each time it overflows its banks.

At one point the retreating ice paused long enough to block the valley near the present village of Lowther Ings, and a temporary lake formed behind it. Fine mud settled on the lake floor in thin layers, one pair of light and dark bands for each summer and winter. When the ice barrier finally gave way the lake drained, but its bed remained as a broad flat basin floored with pale, sticky clay. This basin later became the great water meadows of the Ings, and its clay was dug for bricks and tiles in a later age.

The river that runs through this landscape changes its character from source to mouth. Below Comb Water the young Aldern is a narrow torrent, falling steeply over ledges of gritstone in a series of small cascades. Its bed is a jumble of rounded boulders, and its water is clear but stained the colour of weak tea by peat washed from the moorland above. At Thrang Force, a little more than four miles below the tarn, the river drops over a lip of hard gritstone into a deep plunge pool, having cut a narrow gorge back into the rock behind the fall over thousands of years. The sound of the fall can be heard across the open fell in wet weather, when the river rises quickly after rain.

On reaching the limestone the river loses part of its flow. In dry summers much of the water slips away into fissures in its bed, and for a stretch of about two miles above the village of Skelder the channel may run almost dry, leaving a bare pavement of white stones. The water does not disappear but travels through hidden passages and returns to the surface at a group of strong springs below the village, where it rises cold and clear and remarkably constant in volume through the year. The springs at Skelder, known together as the Boilings, are the most reliable source of water in the valley, and the river below them rarely shrinks however dry the season.

Through the middle valley the river winds across a floodplain of moderate width between wooded slopes. Its bed here is of gravel and cobbles, and it divides into riffles, where shallow water runs quickly over stones, and pools, where it deepens and slows. During floods it shifts its gravel bars and sometimes cuts new channels across the inside of its bends. In the lower valley the gradient becomes very gentle, and the river swings in broad meanders across its plain. It undercuts the outer bank of each bend, where the current is strongest, and builds up beaches of sand and silt on the inner bank, where the current slackens. Over time the bends migrate slowly downstream and outward. When two bends grow close enough together the river breaks through the narrow neck of land between them and abandons the loop, which becomes a still, curved pool or oxbow. Several such pools lie on the plain near Selby Cross, gradually filling with reeds and silt.

The vegetation of the valley after the ice ages developed in stages as the climate warmed. The first plants to colonise the raw glacial ground were low mosses, sedges, grasses and creeping dwarf shrubs, much like those that grow on high mountain tops today. These were followed by birch and pine, and then, as the warmth increased, by hazel, oak, elm, lime and alder. At its greatest extent the woodland covered almost the whole valley except for the highest fell tops, the wettest bogs and the open water. The lower slopes and the valley floor carried a dense, mixed forest of oak and lime with elm on the richer soils and hazel in the understorey. Alder and willow crowded along the riverbanks and in the wet hollows of the floodplain, and it is from the alder that the river is held to take its name, the old form of the word meaning a stream fringed with alders.

On the gritstone fells a different pattern developed. The heavy rainfall of the uplands washed nutrients out of the thin, acidic soils, and as the woods on the high ground thinned, a layer of peat began to form. Peat builds up where the ground stays so wet that dead plant matter cannot rot completely, and on the flatter summits of the Carrow Fells it accumulated slowly, year upon year, until it formed a blanket several feet deep across the tops. Stumps of pine and birch can still be seen in places where streams have cut through the peat to its base, showing that trees once grew where there is now only open moor. The surface of the blanket bog is covered with cotton grass, heather, bilberry and sphagnum moss, and it is broken by wet pools and by deep channels called hags where the peat has been eroded.

The limestone country of the middle valley supported its own distinctive plants. Ash woods grew on the steep scars and in the dry valleys, with an understorey of hazel, hawthorn and bird cherry and a ground layer rich in wild garlic, dog's mercury and early purple orchids. On the thin soils of the open limestone the turf was short and fine and full of small flowering herbs, among them thyme, rockrose, bird's-foot trefoil and blue moor grass. The deep fissures of the limestone pavement held hart's-tongue fern, wood sorrel and herb Robert in their damp shade.

Animal life in the early woodland included red deer, roe deer, wild cattle, wild boar, wolves, brown bears, beavers, otters and a great variety of smaller mammals and birds. Beavers dammed the side streams of the middle valley and created a chain of ponds and marshes along the lower reaches of becks such as Ewen Beck and the Skelder Sike. Salmon and sea trout ran up the river each year from the Wenne to spawn in the clean gravels of the middle and upper reaches, and brown trout and eels lived in the river throughout its length. The marshes and pools of the lower valley were the haunt of herons, bitterns, cranes and great numbers of wildfowl in winter.

The first people to enter the valley came as hunters and gatherers in the period after the ice had gone, moving with the seasons along the river and up onto the fells in pursuit of deer and other game. They camped on the dry gravel terraces of the lower valley and on knolls overlooking the river in the middle reaches, and they left behind scatters of small, finely worked flint blades and points, along with the ashes of their hearths. Flint does not occur naturally in the Aldern basin, and the pieces that these people used had been carried in from the chalk country far to the south and east. On the fells they made use of the open ground near the tree line, where game could be watched and followed, and a few of their small camps have been found on spurs above Carrow Comb and near the head of Thrang Gill, where shelter, water and wide views could be had together.

These early inhabitants made only slight changes to the woodland, though they may have used fire to clear small glades where grazing animals would gather and where hazel would grow vigorously for its nuts. Over many generations their way of life slowly gave way to another, in which people began to keep livestock, grow cereal crops and settle more permanently in one place. With that change the long transformation of the Aldern valley from wildwood to farmed land began.
